title: Preservatives, pH, stability tests and honest labels
course_title: Natural Skincare: Basic Creams, Lotions and Facial Oils

say: Preservatives, pH, stability tests and honest labels.
This is the video for module three of Natural Skincare.
Your cream is mostly water. Bacteria, yeasts and moulds can grow in it, often with no sign you can see or smell at first.

panel.heading: Safe before it is sold
items: Germs can grow unseen in water

say: A broad-spectrum preservative controls all three, but only when it is dosed correctly and kept within its pH range.

say: A cream can look perfect on day one and separate weeks later. So you test before you sell, and you write labels that tell the truth.

say: Buy your preservative from a supplier who gives a technical data sheet. Copy four facts. First, the usage rate. Liquid Germall Plus, for example, is used at 0.1 to 0.5 percent.

panel.heading: Four facts from the data sheet

say: Second, the pH range where it works. For Liquid Germall Plus, pH 3 to 8.

panel.heading: Four facts from the data sheet

say: Third, the maximum temperature. Liquid Germall Plus tolerates heat up to 50 degrees, so it goes in at cool-down.

panel.heading: Four facts from the data sheet

say: Fourth, any restrictions, and its INCI name for your label. Remember, vitamin E, honey, salt and essential oils do not replace a preservative in a cream.

panel.heading: Four facts from the data sheet

say: Measure pH the next day, at room temperature, on a small sample, never by dipping into the whole batch. For example, Toyin in Abeokuta has a 500 g cream. Her preservative works best below pH 5.5, but her reading is 6.4.

panel.heading: Toyin brings her cream into range
items: Make 50% citric acid: 5 g in 5 g water

say: She dissolves 5 g of citric acid in 5 g of distilled water, making a 50 percent solution in a labelled bottle.

panel.heading: Toyin brings her cream into range
items: Make 50% citric acid: 5 g in 5 g water

say: She adds 3 drops, stirs for two minutes, and measures a fresh sample: 6.0.

panel.heading: Toyin brings her cream into range
items: Make 50% citric acid: 5 g in 5 g water

say: 3 more drops give 5.6. 2 more give 5.2, inside the range.

panel.heading: Toyin brings her cream into range
items: Make 50% citric acid: 5 g in 5 g water

say: She writes it on the batch sheet, so next time she knows roughly how much a 500 g batch needs.

panel.heading: Toyin brings her cream into range
items: Make 50% citric acid: 5 g in 5 g water

say: Citric acid can sting eyes and broken skin. Wear gloves, label the solution, and keep it away from children.

panel.heading: Toyin brings her cream into range
items: Make 50% citric acid: 5 g in 5 g water
panel.rule: Add acid in drops, never by pouring. Re-measure every time.

say: Fill small, sanitised, identical jars from the same batch, and label each with the batch code.

panel.heading: The three-temperature test
items: Fill 4 identical jars from one batch
Room, fridge at about 4°C, warm 40 to 45°C
Keep the fourth sealed as reference
Look, smell, feel and measure pH

say: Keep one at room temperature, one in a fridge at about 4 degrees, and one in a warm place at 40 to 45 degrees. Heat speeds up failure, so the warm jar often shows problems first.

say: Keep a fourth jar sealed and untouched, as your reference.

say: Check at 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 weeks.

say: Each time, look for separation, smell for sourness, feel the thickness, and measure pH. For example, Uche in Aba saw her version with 5 percent e-wax separate in the warm jar by week 4, while 6 percent stayed unchanged.

say: If any sample shows mould, fuzzy spots or a sour smell, do not use or sell anything from that batch. And never print a shelf life longer than your tests support.

panel.rule: Any mould or sour smell: stop. Do not use or sell that batch.

say: Creams are the product most often used to hide harmful toning ingredients. Never add hydroquinone or mercury compounds.

cards.d: Never add hydroquinone or mercury compounds to any cream.
No steroid, antibiotic or antifungal creams, no crushed tablets. That makes an unregistered medicine.
Do not claim to treat eczema, acne or dark spots. A preserved cream is not preservative-free.

say: Never add steroid creams, antibiotic or antifungal creams, crushed tablets or any medicine. If a customer asks you to add something strong, say no. You make cosmetic moisturisers only.

cards.d: Never add hydroquinone or mercury compounds to any cream.
No steroid, antibiotic or antifungal creams, no crushed tablets. That makes an unregistered medicine.
Do not claim to treat eczema, acne or dark spots. A preserved cream is not preservative-free.

say: And say only what is true. A cream moisturises and softens. It does not treat eczema, acne or dark spots. A cream with a preservative is not preservative-free.

No steroid, antibiotic or antifungal creams, no crushed tablets. That makes an unregistered medicine.

say: List ingredients by their INCI names, largest first, with every part of the emulsifying wax and preservative. Water becomes Aqua. Add the net weight, and a batch code on every jar.
Add dates, directions, and for external use only.
Name nut oils, fragrance and preservatives, and print patch test before first use. Add your name and address.
To sell, NAFDAC registration needs business registration, trademark evidence, a premises inspection, a compliant label and a lab certificate of analysis.
To remember. Water means a broad-spectrum preservative, and the cream's pH must sit in its range. Adjust in drops.
Test at three temperatures and keep batch records. And never add medicines or make false claims.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Cream pH inside the preservative's range
Test at three temperatures; record batches
No medicines, no false claims, INCI labels

say: Now make your preservative fact card and pH record, start a four-jar stability test, and draft a compliant cream label.
